page.title: Capacity and memory
page.description: A tinyactors actor takes about 530 bytes started and 120 hibernated, and each operation costs about the same at four million actors as at two.

hero.headline: Fit millions of actors in one process
hero.lede: On Node.js a started actor takes about 530 bytes and a hibernated one about 120, so four million fit in one process. Each operation costs about the same at four million actors as at two.

section.heading: Let the host grow its memory
section.p: A host keeps the actors of each compiled image in one block of memory, its region. When one of its pools fills, actors or timers for instance, the host copies the region into a larger one.
A host given no sizes starts with room for 64 actors, and grows as the population does.

section.heading: Set where each pool starts
section.p: The system map of the config option gives each new region its first sizes, in whole numbers. An absent key, or 0, keeps the default.

row.cell: events waiting in the actors' queues
actors in the middle of a step at once (a sender keeps its workspace until its send is handled); never refused: an actor waits for one, and the host adds more
derived from the image and maxActors

section.p: A size is where a pool starts, and the host still grows it. A pool that fills grows between runs, and the other pools stay as they were.

item.text: A pool doubles, or grows up to 16 times at once when doubling would add under a quarter of the region. So a small pool beside a large region grows in a few copies.
maxActors is at most 8,388,606. A run or an input is refused with TA_ERROR_NO_MEMORY only at a pool's largest size, or when the allocator refuses memory.

section.heading: See how full each pool is
section.p: await host.hostStats() answers with pools, one entry per region still in use (). An entry's segment is its image's place among new Host's charts, or what addImage returned.
Each pool reports its capacity, what it holds in used, and the most it held at once in highWater.
The pools are actors, events, timers, workspaces, requests and slabBytes, the memory for the actors' variables and strings.
A thousand idle actors grow a host that starts at the default 64, and fit in one sized for 1000. Each region grows on its own, so a second image is a second entry.

example.code: maxActors default: capacity 64, then 1000 used, high water 1000, grown: true segments reported: 0, 1 maxActors 1000: capacity 1000, then 1000 used, high water 1000, grown: false segments reported: 0, 1

section.p: A migration's old and new versions are two entries too, one per image.

section.heading: Size a host for a known population
section.p: Run a realistic load, read the high-water marks, and give the next host those sizes. A host sized for its load makes no copies, and no pool grows past what the load needs.
Count every actor in maxActors, since a hibernated one keeps its slot and its record, about 64 bytes. Size instanceBytes and stringBytes for the resident actors only.
The repository's hibernation gate sizes a host this way for two million counters of a few variables, 1000 resident at most. host.hostConfig() answers the sizes, every default filled in.
A chart with more variables or longer strings needs more per resident actor. slabBytes.highWater under load shows how much.

section.heading: Leave room for pools that fill together
section.p: A pending delayed send holds a timer and an event, and one falling due briefly holds a second event. So N actors that each wait on a delayed send need maxTimers of N and maxEvents above it.
Actors that become runnable together each hold a workspace, against a default of 4. Timers due in the same tick do, and so do actors sending to each other.
On @tinyactors/wasm a pool that runs out costs most: the region is copied inside WebAssembly memory, which keeps its peak.

section.p: That host reached 35 workspaces at once. A million actors sending to each other reached 92.

section.heading: Measure what one actor costs
section.p: The memory program measures the resident memory that one more actor, message or delayed send adds to a process. Run it with your chart, on your runtime and datamodel, the engine chart code runs in: native or quickjs.

table.caption: A million actors. Measured 2026-11-20 on an Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, 4 CPUs, 16 GiB, Linux; Node.js 22.23.5 and Bun 1.4.1. A counter chart with one <data>, messages of {"text": "hello"}, tracing on; the hibernated column keeps at most 1000 actors resident and the rest in a store.

section.p: On Node.js a started actor takes 531 B at a million, and a hibernated one 124 B. The host's and the engine's fixed costs spread over the population, so an actor costs less in a larger one.

table.caption: Per actor at each population, Node.js on the native datamodel, the same run.

section.p: The run's CSV holds every row at every population and on every runtime, to compare with your own chart's.

item.text: holds its variables in the datamodel and its records in the region: 196 B for this chart at a million (81 B, its instance and its strings).
an actor keeps that event as _event until the next one.
keeps only its records in the region, 81 B to 89 B, and its blob is in your store: 145 B on the native datamodel and 147 B on quickjs, for this chart.
costs 106 B in the region (57 B with tracing off) and its data in the datamodel.
holds its message until it falls due: 151 B in the region (102 B with tracing off).

the engine keeps every actor's variables in its own heap, bounded by quickjs.memoryLimit, 1 GiB unless the host sets another. A million resident actors after an event need about 1.2 GB of it, so the run above sets 8 GiB (the quickjs sandbox).

section.p: A chart's scripts add nothing per actor. Their functions are the chart's, made once, and a top-level var is one more variable (Writing charts).

section.heading: Check that costs hold as actors double
section.p: The scaling program, tools/scale.mjs, times every operation on N actors and on 2N, each host in its own process. It fails an operation that costs more than 1.5 times as much at 2N.
An operation on one actor is timed per call, and one on the whole population per actor.
In the first run most actors are hibernated in SQLite, and one in a hundred runs an invoked service. In the second every actor is resident.
Every operation passed. Each cell is the cost at N, then at 2N, in microseconds, and their ratio.

table.section: Work does not grow with the population
table.caption: Hibernated: 2,000,000 and 4,000,000 actors, at most 1000 counters resident, 20,000 and 40,000 actors each running an invoked service. One run, alone on the machine, 2026-11-20: an Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, 4 CPUs, 16 GiB, Linux; Node.js 22.23.5 and Bun 1.4.1.

table.section: Work does not grow with the population
table.caption: All resident: 1,000,000 and 2,000,000 actors, the same run.

section.p: Two million resident actors take up to 5.2 GiB on quickjs, the most of any run. So four million resident do not fit in 16 GiB beside the scenario's other work.

table.caption: Peak resident memory at N and 2N, in MiB, the same run.

section.p: mise run scale in tinyactors-napi writes every operation and sample to build/scale-*.json. This run's files are in tools/results/2026-11-20.
The repository's rules for published numbers say when to run it again, before each release among them.
